summary:
ANCASH DEPARTMENT STANDS UNDER THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK OF PERU. The source inventory contains no trans-specific ordinance, departmental decree or incident series for Ancash; every usable item is national in scope, and the national framework below is what a visitor to Ancash is scored against.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting entry into public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to a person's birth sex. The text carried narrow exceptions for custody situations and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The article notes the text still required plenary backing at that point, and reports the trigger as a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

Activist Gianna Camacho is quoted arguing that the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The IDEHPUCP legal analysis of 15 April 2025, by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors.

Enforcement reaches private premises as well as state facilities. SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI.

Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, so a visitor cannot rely on documentary recognition to settle which facilities are open to them.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases across 2020 to 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023.

One 2023 case illustrates the pattern: in February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by the Los Gallegos extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023.

The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.
tangentialFactors:
Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law; Congress voted in 2017 to strip those protections from the new Penal Code, the repeal carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, a standard Peru's bathroom statute sits against.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the regional human-rights court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history.

Two protective developments are on record: in June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, and in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

The bathroom restriction's stated trigger, the July 2023 complaint about restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport, is a Lima event; no equivalent Ancash dispute appears in the inventory.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same Article 5.1 restriction as visitors, but additionally carry the burden of gender-identity recognition, which in Peru remains a long, costly and invasive procedure before a court.

Discrimination complaints are routed through the consumer-protection body INDECOPI, whose record is weak: Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's complaint against SmartFit after the gym relied on the sex recorded in the DNI. A consumer-protection body likewise dismissed a trans woman's complaint against a gym enforcing the national policy.

Because sexual orientation and gender identity are absent from the state's crime-registration systems, residents reporting an anti-trans attack cannot have it recorded or prosecuted as a hate crime.

Enforcement of the restroom restriction extends into broadcast media and public speech: television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Ancash-specific source appears in the inventory: no departmental ordinance, regional health directive, municipal resolution, police report or documented incident for Ancash is available to verify how the national bathroom statute is applied in Huaraz or elsewhere in the department. Enforcement practice in Ancash is therefore unresolved rather than absent.

Whether venues in Ancash have been required to remove ambiguous restroom signs, and whether security staff there check the DNI at restroom doors, is not sourced.

The 2020 to 2023 killing figures are national and are not broken down by department in the inventory, so no Ancash-specific count of anti-trans homicides can be stated.

The inventory does not record whether the February 2025 dictamen's exceptions for custody and for accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities have been applied in Ancash, nor whether the April 2025 law has been challenged locally.

Regional court rulings, the July 2025 Lima constitutional decision and the December 2025 Azul Rojas Marín sentence are national or capital-based; their citation in Ancash is as national context, not as local precedent.
